description: For this NASA Space Apps challenge, we are building SmartVitals AI—an autonomous, edge-AI health monitoring dashboard designed for astronauts on long-duration space missions (like Artemis or Mars trips) where communication with Earth has a 20-minute delay.
summary: SmartVitals is a student prototype for monitoring astronaut health on deep-space missions, where communication delays rule out real-time guidance from Earth. The system streams four simulated vital signs (heart rate, SpO₂, body temperature, and a stress index), detects anomalies locally with an Isolation Forest model plus threshold rules, and logs events in SQLite so records persist offline. It includes a live crew dashboard and a simulated Earth-link toggle. It’s a decision-support concept only, using synthetic data, and not a medical device.

SmartVitals: S.M.A.R.T. Vitals is a student project from Dayananda Sagar University (team SmartVitals) that proposes offline health monitoring for astronauts on deep-space missions. Because radio delay makes real-time guidance from Earth impractical, the system runs on the spacecraft itself, analyzing vital signs locally and keeping records without any network connection.

The deck opens with the mission context. Communication delay prevents real-time medical advice from Earth, astronaut vitals fluctuate quickly with microgravity workload and sleep, and health records need to persist without external links. From this, the prototype sets four objectives: collect simulated vital-sign streams, analyze them locally for multi-vital anomalies, alert the crew with clear trends, and record events offline in SQLite.

The telemetry and workflow slide covers four monitored channels: SpO₂ (an oxygen saturation estimate), heart rate (a simulated BPM pulse), body temperature (core Celsius), and a stress index (a synthetic 0–100 workload score). These feed a four-step loop of Collect, Analyze, Alert, and Record.

The architecture slide describes the stack: a simulator producing NumPy vital arrays, a FastAPI backend for orchestration, an Isolation Forest model from scikit-learn for anomaly detection, a SQLite database for persistent history, and a Chart.js live dashboard. Anomaly detection is hybrid, combining the Isolation Forest with deterministic threshold rules. The deck is explicit that this flags statistical outliers in synthetic data and does not make clinical diagnoses.

The interface showcase shows a live crew dashboard for "Astronaut 01" with a status banner reading "Local AI Active • Earth Delayed," a sample SQLite event log of timestamped readings marked NOMINAL, and interactive controls for testing anomaly alerts, pausing the stream, and simulating Earth-link states.

The scope and roadmap slide separates what exists from what's planned. The current prototype uses synthetic data without physical sensors, runs inference and storage on-device, and includes a simulated Earth link toggle. Planned work includes benchmarking against public physiological datasets, personalizing anomaly thresholds per astronaut, and adding a buffer-and-replay system to sync queued telemetry after an outage. The deck closes with a safety principle: this is a decision-support concept only and does not replace qualified flight surgeons or mission protocols.
